stocks.note: Numbers as of market close on Friday, May 15th.
stocks.news: All three indices closed sharply lower into the weekend with the S&P pulling back to 7,408 (-1.24%), DOW retreating to 49,526 (-1.07%), and Nasdaq down 1.54% to 26,225. The headline story going into Monday: Bill Ackman is buying the Microsoft (MSFT +3.05%) dip. Pershing Square (PS -3.38%) revealed it loaded up on MSFT shares this year while the stock has fallen 26% from its October 2025 high on AI-spend worries. Ackman argues the company's AI and cloud business remains structurally strong and undervalued, and Microsoft popped 3% on Friday on his disclosure. For market-watching clients, the read is straightforward: the smart-money playbook right now is to look through the AI-capex anxiety to the underlying earnings power.

economy.note: US 10-Year and Gold as of 4:00 PM ET May 17th; WTI Crude reflects today's intraday move via investing.com.
economy.commentary:
The macro picture into Monday is that the economy is staying hot, not cooling. The 10-year edged up to 4.62%, gold pulled back 1.11% to $4,511 as risk-off bid faded, and WTI Crude is up another 1.25% to $102.28. Brent is at $111.78, a meaningful spread that reflects the Iran-war energy premium still feeding through.

The headline data point of the week: U.S. factories just posted their best month in over a year. Industrial production rose 0.7% in April, with motor vehicles and parts jumping 3.7%. The chart above is the FRED series, and the slope tells the story. Three years of essentially flat factory output, then a sharp upward break starting in late 2025 that has continued through Q1 2026. Oil shocks and rising bond yields have not slowed activity yet.

The other shoe drops in the inflation outlook. The Philly Fed's panel of forecasters now expects CPI to hit 6% this quarter, up from 2.7% in February, with the Iran-war oil premium being cited as the trigger. Whether the panel is right or wrong, what matters for rates is that consensus is moving the wrong direction. A resilient economy plus a rising-inflation outlook is the worst possible mix for the rate-cut thesis that 2025's bull run was built on.

For client conversations, the takeaway is the same one we have been carrying for two weeks: do not let any buyer or seller anchor on "rates will come down soon." The data is no longer cooperating with that narrative.

crypto.note: Numbers as of 4:00 PM ET on May 17th.
crypto.commentary:
Crypto cooled across the board over the weekend. BTC pulled back to $76,846 (-0.72%), ETH at $2,109 (-0.88%), and XRP at $1.39 (-1.00%). BTC is now down about 5% from Thursday's $81,040 close on the back of the broader risk-off move in stocks.

The story worth flagging for clients who follow crypto: Strategy (MSTR -5.11%), the largest corporate Bitcoin holder on earth with $63B in BTC, just filed to buy back $1.5B of its debt and explicitly listed Bitcoin sales as one of the funding options. Michael Saylor famously said in 2021 that Strategy would never sell Bitcoin. That "never sell" thesis was a load-bearing piece of the Bitcoin bull case for years. The filing does not commit Strategy to selling, but it puts the option on the table for the first time, and the stock dropped 5% on the news.

On the institutional adoption side, Mastercard (MA +0.87%) agreed to buy BVNK, a payments-rails service that links crypto wallets to traditional bank accounts. That is the kind of plumbing-level deal that meaningfully expands the practical use cases for crypto in everyday commerce.

real_estate.homebuilder: Rates Tick Up Into Monday At 6.65%, Industrial Production Surge Keeps Rate-Cut Path Closed, Gen Z Quietly Becomes 20% Of Buy Demand
real_estate.commentary:
Three threads to open the week with clients.

First, rates ticked up over the weekend. The 30-year is at 6.65%, up 3 bps from Friday's 6.62%. The 15-year is at 6.10%, up 1 bp. Modest moves, but the direction matters. Five days ago we were at 6.42% on the 30-year. We are 23 bps higher than that in a week, the largest weekly move we have tracked this year, and the rates have now ticked up again on the Monday open rather than mean-reverting. The bond market is not done repricing.

Second, the macro is no longer working in favor of the rate-cut narrative. April industrial production rose 0.7% (chart in the Economy section above), the strongest single-month reading in over a year, with motor vehicles and parts up 3.7%. The Philly Fed's forecaster panel now expects CPI to hit 6% this quarter, up from 2.7% in February. A resilient economy plus a rising inflation forecast is the exact macro mix that closes the rate-cut window. The CME Fed-cut odds for 2026 sat at 1.6% as of Friday. Nothing in this morning's data moves that number higher. Any client telling you they are waiting for cuts is making a bet against a 98.4% probability.

Third, the demographic story worth flagging on buyer calls this week: Gen Z is now responsible for almost 20% of U.S. mortgage buy requests, per LendingTree. The interesting wrinkle is where they are buying. Minneapolis, Birmingham, and Indianapolis are the biggest Gen Z destinations. Miami, San Francisco, and Las Vegas are showing essentially no Gen Z interest. The under-30 cohort is voting with its feet against coastal-and-large-city pricing. For Bay Area listings, the implication is that the pool of demand from that age bracket is structurally smaller than it would have been five years ago. The buyers coming to the table here remain dominated by older move-up and equity-rich households. Price your listings and shape your messaging accordingly.

Total active inventory across the 15-city board is 2,955, down 12 from Friday. 275 new listings on the board this morning, up from Friday's 250 as the weekend backlog hits the active count. 238 closed sales for the rolling 7-day window, up from Friday's 223 as the window rolled forward through the weekend. The composition of the day is unmistakable: Oakland, Danville, Pleasanton, and Hayward are the four cities loading product into the active count. For listing agents working those cities, you are pricing into a heavier supply backdrop today than Friday.

For listing agents: the rate story is your story today. 30-year +23 bps in a week, +3 bps over the weekend, Fed cuts at 1.6% odds for the year. Any seller you talk to this week who is still anchored to "rates will come down before I list" is sitting on a position the bond market has already rejected. Send a written touchpoint to every active prospect with those three numbers.

For buyer agents: 275 new listings on the board this morning is a real supply pulse. The selection is genuinely better today than it was on Friday, particularly in Oakland (+11), Danville (+6), Pleasanton (+4), and Hayward (+3). Active buyers who pulled back over the weekend lost a little ground on selection but gained almost nothing on pricing. The math for them is unchanged: rates are not getting better in their timeframe, and inventory is finally moving.
